en.title: Quantity Surveying: the whole course
en.short: What quantity surveying covers, how QS degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What quantity surveying is
sections.text:
Quantity surveying is the construction profession that manages cost, measurement and contract matters. A quantity surveyor measures work from drawings, prepares bills of quantities (itemised lists of work and quantities for pricing) and estimates, plans and controls cost, procures contractors, values work done, agrees changes and settles final accounts. The surveyor also handles claims, risk, cash flow and feasibility studies.

It is not only counting. You must understand how a building or a road is actually built, because the method and sequence of construction decide what is measured and how it is priced.

Quantity surveyors work for consultancies, contractors, clients, developers and government. Rules, standard bills, contract forms and registration differ by country. In Nigeria the profession is regulated by the Quantity Surveyors Registration Board of Nigeria, with the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors as the professional body. In the UK the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors is a leading body. Check the current rules where you plan to practise.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria a BSc in quantity surveying commonly takes four years. Polytechnic students take an ND (National Diploma), then industrial training, then an HND (Higher National Diploma). In the UK a full-time BSc usually takes three years, and sandwich routes take longer. Master’s degrees usually take one to two years.

The early years are shared: mathematics, construction technology, technical drawing, materials, measurement principles and construction economics. The middle years carry the core: measurement of substructure, superstructure, finishes, services and civil works, bills of quantities, estimating, tendering, contracts and administration. Later years add claims, cost control, project management, property development and professional practice. Most courses end with a final-year project, and a master’s adds advanced economics, digital tools, sustainability and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Start with the setting: what the profession does, how buildings are put together, how to read drawings and schedules, the main materials, and the mathematics you will use. Statistics and ICT with CAD come here too, because measurement software is now normal.

Then learn the principles of measurement: how rules work, what is measured, and how descriptions are written. Practise on simple building works before moving to substructure, superstructure, finishes, joinery and building services. Civil engineering measurement follows, with its own rules for earthworks, roads, drainage and structures.

Next comes cost: estimating and cost planning, bills of quantities, tendering and procurement, contracts and law, contract administration and valuation. Then claims and dispute resolution, cost control and cash flow, project management and risk, and property development and feasibility.

Professional practice and ethics run alongside, and the final-year project pulls the skills together. At master’s level come advanced construction economics, digital surveying and building information modelling (BIM), sustainable construction and carbon costing, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Measure something every week. Take a simple drawing and produce a measured description by hand, then check it against a worked example or your lecturer’s model answer. Keep a file of your take-off sheets (your measurement workings) and learn from the errors.

Learn the units and the order of measurement, and write descriptions in the standard form your syllabus uses. Read drawings until you can see the building in your head. Visit sites and ask how each element is actually built and priced.

Practise arithmetic without a calculator sometimes, and always check totals. Use software only after you can do the method by hand.

keyPoints: Quantity surveying manages cost, measurement and contracts from design through to final account.
Understand construction methods, because they decide what is measured and how it is priced.

en.title: Introduction to Quantity Surveying
en.short: The quantity surveyor’s role, history, work areas, careers and country-specific regulation.

sections.heading: The role
sections.text: A quantity surveyor is a construction professional who advises on cost, value, procurement and contracts. The role sits in the construction team beside the client, architect, engineer and contractor. The surveyor helps the client know what a project should cost, choose how to buy the work, and keep spending under control. The title is protected in some countries but not all, so check local rules.

sections.heading: How it grew
sections.text: Quantity surveying grew in Britain during the nineteenth century. As buildings became larger and contracts more complex, builders and clients needed measured lists of work and agreed prices. Bills of quantities and independent measurement developed from that need. The profession later spread through the Commonwealth and elsewhere, adapting to local laws and markets. Its history explains its focus on fair, documented measurement and cost.

sections.heading: Main work areas
sections.text: Measurement means taking quantities from drawings and specifications. Cost work includes early estimates, cost plans, budgets and cost control. Procurement is deciding how work is bought and which contractor is chosen, often through tendering. Contract advice covers the contract conditions, valuations, variations and claims. Many surveyors specialise, for example in building, civil engineering, services or dispute work.

sections.heading: Careers and regulation
sections.text: A surveyor may work for a consultancy, contractor, public client, developer, bank or university. Professional bodies include RICS in the United Kingdom, NIQS in Nigeria and ASAQS in South Africa. Regulators include QSRBN in Nigeria and SACQSP in South Africa. Registration rules differ by country; some titles are protected. Example: Ada in Enugu works for a consultant QS firm. She measures a school block, prepares a cost plan, and later checks the contractor’s monthly valuation.

keyPoints: A quantity surveyor advises on construction cost, value, procurement and contracts.
The profession grew from nineteenth-century British practice of measuring work and preparing bills of quantities.
Main work areas are measurement, cost planning and control, procurement and contract advice.
Quantity surveyors work for consultants, contractors, clients, developers, banks and universities.
Professional bodies and regulators are country-specific, for example RICS in the UK, NIQS and QSRBN in Nigeria.
Registration rules and protected titles differ by country, so check the current local requirements.

en.title: Construction Technology: Building Elements and Methods
en.short: Building elements from foundations to finishes, and how drawings and specifications describe them.

sections.heading: Substructure and foundations
sections.text: The substructure is the part below ground, including foundations. It transfers building loads to the soil. A foundation must be strong enough for the load and the ground, and deep enough to avoid damage from swelling, shrinkage or erosion. Common shallow foundations are strip footings under walls, pad footings under columns, and rafts, which spread load over a wide area. Deep foundations, such as piles, reach stronger soil or rock. The method depends on ground conditions, load and local practice. Codes differ by country; check local code.

sections.heading: Walls and floors
sections.text: The superstructure is the part above ground: walls, columns, beams, floors and roof. Walls may be load-bearing, carrying floors and roof, or non-load-bearing partitions. Wall methods are blockwork, brickwork, in-situ concrete and timber stud. A cavity wall has two leaves with a gap, for insulation or damp control. Ground floors may be concrete slabs laid on hardcore and a damp-proof membrane. Upper floors are suspended: reinforced concrete slabs, timber joists or precast units. Columns and beams carry loads to foundations.

sections.heading: Roofs and finishes
sections.text: Roofs are pitched or flat. A pitched roof uses rafters or trusses and a covering such as tiles or metal sheets. A flat roof needs a waterproof membrane and falls to drains. Finishes include screed on floors, plaster or render on walls, tiling, and paint. Finishes protect the structure and give a usable surface. Their specification names the material, thickness, preparation and workmanship.

sections.heading: Drawings and specifications
sections.text: Drawings show location, size and levels. Plans show layout; sections show heights and construction; elevations show external faces; detail drawings show junctions. Schedules list repeated items such as doors and windows. The specification states materials, standards and workmanship. Together they describe the work so it can be measured and costed. A clinic in Ibadan might have strip footings, sandcrete block walls, suspended concrete floor and timber truss roof. These are described on drawings and in the specification.

keyPoints: Substructure transfers loads to the ground; superstructure includes walls, columns, floors and roof.
Shallow foundations include strip, pad and raft; deep foundations include piles.
Walls may be load-bearing or non-load-bearing; floors may be ground-bearing or suspended.
Pitched roofs use rafters or trusses; flat roofs need waterproofing and falls to drains.
Finishes such as screed, plaster, tiling and paint protect the structure and give a usable surface.
Drawings and specifications describe location, materials and workmanship so work can be measured and costed; codes differ by country.

en.title: Reading Building Drawings and Schedules
en.short: Plans, sections, elevations, details, schedules, scales, symbols and checking drawings for quantities.

sections.heading: Views and scales
sections.text: A plan is a view from above of a horizontal cut through a building. A section is a vertical cut, showing heights and construction. An elevation shows an outside face. A detail drawing enlarges a small part, such as a junction. Scales are ratios: at 1:50, one unit on the drawing represents 50 units in reality. At 1:100 it represents 100. Check the stated scale and the title block before measuring.

sections.heading: Symbols and dimensions
sections.text: Symbols include door swings, windows, grid lines, level marks, section markers and a north arrow. Building dimensions are usually written in millimetres, but confirm the unit on the drawing. Use figured dimensions, not scaled measurements, for quantities. Example: a room measures 80 mm by 60 mm on a 1:50 plan. Actual length = 80 × 50 = 4,000 mm = 4.0 m; width = 60 × 50 = 3,000 mm = 3.0 m; area = 4.0 × 3.0 = 12.0 m².

sections.heading: Schedules and quantities
sections.text: Schedules are tables that list repeated items: doors, windows, rooms, finishes or reinforcement. They give marks, sizes, materials and quantities. To extract quantities, count items, read figured lengths, calculate areas from dimensions, and take volumes from sections and levels. Write descriptions from the drawings and schedules together. For the room above, floor finish area is 12.0 m²; skirting length is 2 × (4.0 + 3.0) = 14.0 m, less door openings.

sections.heading: Checking drawings
sections.text: Before taking off, check the title block, drawing number, revision and date. Compare plans, sections, elevations and schedules for missing or conflicting information. A door may be shown on plan but absent from the door schedule; a dimension on one drawing may conflict with the same dimension on another. Mark queries and send a request for information (RFI). Do not guess. Drawing conventions and design codes differ by country and office, so follow the project’s stated conventions and the current local code.

keyPoints: A plan is a horizontal cut viewed from above; a section is a vertical cut; an elevation shows an outside face.
At scale 1:n, real length = drawing length × n, using the same units.
Use figured dimensions rather than scaling drawings for quantities.
Schedules list repeated items such as doors, windows and finishes and must agree with the drawings.
Extract quantities by counting, measuring lengths, calculating areas and taking volumes from levels and sections.
Check title block, revisions and conflicts, and issue an RFI rather than guessing.

en.title: Construction Materials for Quantity Surveyors
en.short: Properties, uses, units and measurement effects of concrete, steel, timber, masonry, finishes and insulation.

sections.heading: Properties and units
sections.text:
Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension; its grade, density and workability affect use. It is measured in cubic metres (m³) for slabs, beams and foundations. Steel has high tensile strength and stiffness; reinforcement is measured in kilograms or tonnes, and structural sections are often measured by length and converted to mass using their mass per metre (kg/m).

Timber is strong for its weight but shrinks and swells with moisture; it is measured in cubic metres for volume or linear metres for mouldings. Masonry units, such as blocks and bricks, are measured in square metres for walls and cubic metres for thick work. Finishes are measured in square metres, using coverage and thickness. Insulation is measured in square metres with a stated thickness, or cubic metres; its thermal conductivity (W/m·K) matters. Grades and standards differ by country, so check the project specification and local standards.

sections.heading: Measurement and wastage
sections.text:
Measurement starts from drawn dimensions, not from assumed sizes. Nominal sizes may differ from actual sizes, especially for timber and masonry. Density converts volume to mass, which matters for steel and transport. Wastage covers cutting, breakage and over-order. It is usually added as a percentage that varies with material, detail and site practice; check the specification or company data.

Example: a concrete slab 5.0 m × 4.0 m × 0.15 m has net volume 5.0 × 4.0 × 0.15 = 3.00 m³. A 5% wastage allowance gives 3.00 × 1.05 = 3.15 m³. At a made-up rate of ₦80,000 per m³, cost = 3.15 × 80,000 = ₦252,000.

sections.heading: Specification and cost
sections.text:
Specification fixes the grade, size and finish, and so affects the unit rate. A higher concrete grade or a better timber species costs more but may reduce thickness or maintenance.

The quantity surveyor should measure net quantities, state the wastage basis, and price transport and waste separately where needed. Material prices change by place and time, so use current supplier quotations.

keyPoints: Concrete is measured in m³, steel in kg or tonnes, timber in m³ or m, masonry in m² or m³, and finishes and insulation in m² with stated thickness.
Properties such as strength, density, moisture content and thickness affect specification, measurement and cost.
Measure from drawn dimensions, and check nominal against actual sizes when ordering; convert volume to mass with density where needed.
Quantity including waste = net quantity × (1 + wastage rate).
Cost = quantity including waste × unit rate, with transport and waste priced where required.
Grades, standards and wastage allowances vary by country and project, so check the specification and current supplier quotations.

en.title: Mathematics for Quantity Surveying
en.short: Arithmetic, algebra, areas, volumes, percentages, ratios and simple interest for construction measurement.

sections.heading: Numbers and algebra
sections.text: Arithmetic means confident use of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, powers and roots. Algebra uses letters for unknown quantities and follows the same rules. In estimating, a formula is a recipe: substitute known values, keep units consistent, then check the answer by rough estimation. For example, a concrete mix of 1:2:4 by volume has 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 parts. For 3.5 m³ of concrete, cement volume = (1 ÷ 7) × 3.5 = 0.5 m³. This is a simplified volume guide; in practice the dry materials add up to more than the finished volume, and waste varies.

sections.heading: Areas and volumes
sections.text: Geometry gives the shapes behind measurement. Rectangle area = length × breadth; triangle area = 0.5 × base × height; circle area = πr². Volume of a rectangular prism = length × breadth × height. A wall 6.0 m long and 2.7 m high has gross area 6.0 × 2.7 = 16.2 m². A window 1.2 m × 1.5 m = 1.8 m² is deducted, leaving 14.4 m². A footing 2.0 m × 0.6 m × 0.25 m has volume 2.0 × 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.30 m³. Metres give square metres and cubic metres.

sections.heading: Percentages, ratios, interest
sections.text: A percentage is a fraction of 100. To add 5% waste to 14.4 m², multiply by 1.05: 14.4 × 1.05 = 15.12 m². A ratio compares quantities; a proportion states that two ratios are equal. If 3 m³ of concrete needs 1.5 m³ of sand, then 5 m³ needs 1.5 × 5 ÷ 3 = 2.5 m³. Simple interest is I = P × r × t, where P is principal, r the annual rate as a decimal and t the time in years. A loan of 500,000 at 8% for 2 years gives I = 500,000 × 0.08 × 2 = 80,000. Rates vary, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Rectangle area = length × breadth; rectangular prism volume = length × breadth × height.
Circle area = πr² and triangle area = 0.5 × base × height.
To add a percentage, multiply by 1 + rate ÷ 100.
Simple interest: I = P × r × t, with r as a decimal and t in years.
Ratios and proportions scale quantities; use the same units throughout.
Keep units consistent and check calculations by rough estimation.

en.title: Principles of Measurement
en.short: Purpose, units, taking off, abstracting, billing, waste and deductions in measurement.

sections.heading: Purpose and units
sections.text: Measurement is the process of quantifying construction work from drawings and specifications. Its results support cost planning, tendering, valuation of work done and ordering. A quantity surveyor measures in standard units: length in metres (m), area in square metres (m²), volume in cubic metres (m³), mass in kilograms (kg) or tonnes, and countable items in number (nr). Each item needs a description of material, quality, workmanship and dimensions. Standard methods of measurement set the rules. They differ by country and edition, so use the current edition specified by your institution or professional body.

sections.heading: Taking off
sections.text: Taking off means extracting dimensions from drawings and writing them in a recognised order, usually length, width and height or depth, on dimension paper, a ruled sheet with columns for recording and squaring dimensions. Waste is the allowance for cutting and irregular shapes; the method states when it is added. Deductions remove work not present, such as openings from wall finishes. Rules for small openings vary, so check the edition. Example: a wall 5.000 m long and 2.400 m high has gross area 5.000 × 2.400 = 12.000 m². A door 0.900 m wide and 2.100 m high has area 0.900 × 2.100 = 1.890 m². Net area = 12.000 − 1.890 = 10.110 m².

sections.heading: Abstracting and billing
sections.text: Abstracting collects measured items of the same kind from the take-off into a summary, so quantities can be added and checked. Billing writes the abstracted items into a bill of quantities (BoQ): a document listing descriptions, units and quantities. The BoQ lets tenderers price the same work fairly and later supports valuations and variations. Good practice is to keep descriptions short but complete, use the correct unit, and check dimensions and arithmetic before billing. Measurement is not guesswork: every quantity should be traceable to a drawing, a specification or a clear instruction.

keyPoints: Measurement quantifies work from drawings and specifications for costing, tendering and valuation.
Use the current standard method of measurement specified by your institution or professional body; methods differ by country and edition.
Area = length × width; volume = length × width × depth.
Taking off records dimensions in a recognised order, usually length, width, height or depth.
Net quantity = gross quantity − deductions; add waste only as the method requires.
Abstracting groups like items, and billing sets them out in a bill of quantities with descriptions, units and quantities.

en.title: Measurement of Simple Building Works
en.short: First taking-off of simple excavations, concrete, masonry and finishes with clear descriptions.

sections.heading: Taking off
sections.text: Taking off means transferring dimensions from drawings into measured items. Work element by element in a fixed order, for example excavation, concrete, masonry, finishes. Record each dimension as length × width × height or depth, in metres, and state the unit: m³ for excavation and concrete, m² for walls and finishes, m for linear items. Use the measurement rules given for your project; they decide what is included or deducted. In Nigeria, for example, quantity surveyors commonly follow the Nigerian Standard Method of Measurement of Building Works; other countries have their own. Check the current edition and the project’s stated rules.

sections.heading: Excavation and concrete
sections.text: Example: a trench 12.00 m long, 0.60 m wide and 1.00 m deep. Volume = 12.00 × 0.60 × 1.00 = 7.20 m³. Description: 'Excavate trench for strip footing, 0.60 m wide, depth not exceeding 1.00 m, in ordinary soil.' A strip footing 12.00 m long, 0.60 m wide and 0.20 m thick: concrete volume = 12.00 × 0.60 × 0.20 = 1.44 m³. Description: 'Concrete (1:3:6) in strip footing, 0.20 m thick.' The mix and thickness belong in the description because they affect cost.

sections.heading: Masonry and finishes
sections.text: A wall 12.00 m long and 2.70 m high, 0.225 m thick: area = 12.00 × 2.70 = 32.40 m². Describe as '225 mm brick wall in cement mortar (1:6), 2.70 m high.' Plaster to one side: 32.40 m², described as '12 mm cement-sand plaster (1:4) to wall.' Deduct openings only as the rules require. Keep dimensions in a consistent order and label each item.

sections.heading: Clear descriptions
sections.text: A good description answers what, where, material, mix, thickness and size. Avoid vague words like 'as directed'. Check every calculation and cross-reference to the drawing. The aim is correct technique, not complex work.

keyPoints: Taking off transfers dimensions from drawings into measured items using the given rules.
Volume = length × width × depth; area = length × height.
Use m³ for excavation and concrete, m² for masonry and finishes, m for linear items.
A description states material, mix, thickness, location and size.
Deduct openings only where the measurement rules require it.
Check arithmetic and keep dimensions in a consistent order.

en.title: Construction Economics: An Introduction
en.short: Demand and supply, cost, price and value, the construction market and simple investment appraisal.

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.text: Construction economics applies economic ideas to building. Demand is the quantity clients will buy at a price; supply is what firms offer. In construction, demand is derived: people build because they need homes, offices or roads. It is volatile and affected by interest rates, public budgets and credit. Supply responds slowly because projects need land, approvals, skilled labour and materials. When demand rises faster than supply, prices and rents tend to rise. Location matters: the same building costs more in a crowded city than in a rural area because land, transport and labour differ.

sections.heading: Cost, price and value
sections.text: Cost is what the contractor spends on labour, materials, plant and overheads. Price is what the client pays under a contract. Value is the worth of the completed asset to the owner or user, which may be higher or lower than cost. A quantity surveyor gives cost advice, not a fixed truth. Rates depend on time, location and market conditions. Material prices, labour rates and plant hire change, so always check current local data. A rate copied from an old bill is only a starting point.

sections.heading: Market and appraisal
sections.text:
The construction market often has many small firms and few large ones. Work is often awarded by tender, so competition affects price. Investment appraisal compares costs and benefits over time. Payback period = initial cost ÷ annual net cash inflow. Net present value (NPV) discounts future cash flows: NPV = Σ (cash flow ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ) − initial cost, where r is the discount rate, the rate used to convert future money to present value, and n the year. A positive NPV suggests the project adds value at that rate.

Example in Nigeria: suppose a mixer costs ₦2,000,000 and yields ₦700,000 net each year for four years at 10%. Payback = 2,000,000 ÷ 700,000 = 2.86 years. NPV = −2,000,000 + 700,000 ÷ 1.1 + 700,000 ÷ 1.1² + 700,000 ÷ 1.1³ + 700,000 ÷ 1.1⁴ = ₦218,906, so accept.

keyPoints: Demand in construction is derived and supply responds slowly, so prices move with market conditions.
Cost is the contractor’s outlay, price is what the client pays, and value is the worth to the owner.
Cost advice must be checked against current local prices, labour rates and market conditions.
Payback period = initial cost ÷ annual net cash inflow.
NPV = Σ (cash flow ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ) − initial cost; a positive NPV adds value at the chosen discount rate.
A rate from another time or place is only a guide, not a current price.

en.title: Statistics and Data for Quantity Surveyors
en.short: Collecting, presenting and interpreting construction data: tables, charts, averages, spread, indices and probability.

sections.heading: Collecting and presenting
sections.text:
Quantity surveyors use data such as tender prices, material costs, labour rates and measured quantities. Record the date, location, unit, source and conditions. Published figures differ by country and year, so check the current official source before comparing.

Use tables for exact values and charts for patterns. A histogram shows grouped numerical data; a bar chart compares categories; a scatter plot suggests a relationship between two variables. Label axes and units.

sections.heading: Averages and spread
sections.text:
An average represents a set. The mean is the sum divided by the count; the median is the middle value when ordered; the mode is the most frequent. The mean uses all values but is pulled by outliers. The median resists outliers.

Dispersion measures spread. Range = highest − lowest. Standard deviation is roughly the typical distance from the mean. For a sample, s = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)].

Example tender prices in millions: 40, 44, 45, 50, 61. Mean = 240 ÷ 5 = 48. Median = 45. Range = 61 − 40 = 21. Deviations from 48: −8, −4, −3, 2, 13; squares: 64, 16, 9, 4, 169; sum = 262; s = √(262 ÷ 4) = √65.5 = 8.09 million.

sections.heading: Index numbers
sections.text: An index number compares a value with a base value, usually 100. Index = (current value ÷ base value) × 100. A construction cost index tracks cost change over time. If the base index is 100 and a later index is 125, costs rose by 25%. To update an old estimate: new estimate = old estimate × (new index ÷ old index). Indices show relative change, not absolute prices, and baskets differ by country.

sections.heading: Simple probability
sections.text: Probability is the chance of an event, from 0 to 1. For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. If 3 of 20 similar tenders were below the estimate, the estimated probability is 3 ÷ 20 = 0.15. Small samples give rough estimates only.

keyPoints: Record source, date, location and units when collecting construction data.
Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle ordered value; mode = most frequent value.
Range = highest − lowest; sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)].
Index = (current value ÷ base value) × 100; update estimate = old estimate × (new index ÷ old index).
Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes for equally likely outcomes.
Published cost indices and tender figures differ by country and year, so check the current official source.

en.title: ICT, CAD and Measurement Software
en.short: Spreadsheets, CAD, measurement software and databases, with checking against drawings and rules.

sections.heading: Spreadsheets and databases
sections.text: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells that can hold numbers, text or formulas. Quantity surveyors use it for take-off sheets, summaries and simple cost models. A formula such as =5.0*2.7 calculates an area. Always check that cell references point to the right rows and columns. A simple database is an organised store of records, for example material prices or standard item descriptions. It can be searched and sorted. Spreadsheets can act as small databases, but a database reduces duplicate entry. Keep backups and note the date of price data.

sections.heading: CAD and measurement software
sections.text: Computer-aided design (CAD) software draws and edits building plans, sections and details. Measurement software, sometimes called take-off software, helps count, measure and list quantities from drawings or from dimensions you enter. Some programs link directly to CAD files. Building information modelling (BIM) goes further: it is a digital model that carries information about components, not just lines. At this stage, know that BIM exists and can produce quantities, but it is not a substitute for measurement rules. File formats and software vary, so check compatibility.

sections.heading: Checking the output
sections.text: Software output must be checked against the drawings and the measurement rules. Drawings can be revised; confirm you are using the current revision. Check scale, dimensions and what is included. Measurement rules say what to deduct, what units to use and how to round. Example: a wall 5.0 m long and 2.7 m high has a door 0.9 m by 2.1 m. Gross area = 5.0 × 2.7 = 13.5 m². Door area = 0.9 × 2.1 = 1.89 m². Net area = 13.5 − 1.89 = 11.61 m². If software reports 13.5 m², it has not deducted the door. If it reports 11.6 m², that is 11.61 rounded to one decimal place. Professional registration and codes differ by country; in Nigeria, quantity surveyors register with the Quantity Surveyors Registration Board of Nigeria (QSRBN) and may join the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors (NIQS). Always follow the local rules.

keyPoints: A spreadsheet stores numbers and formulas in cells; check cell references before trusting results.
CAD draws and edits building drawings; measurement software helps compute quantities from drawings or entered dimensions.
A database stores records such as prices or item descriptions for searching and sorting.
BIM is a digital model with component information; at awareness level, it can help with quantities but needs checking.
Always check software output against the current drawing revision and the measurement rules.
Worked check: wall 5.0 m × 2.7 m less door 0.9 m × 2.1 m gives 13.5 − 1.89 = 11.61 m² net area.

en.title: Measurement of Substructure and Earthworks
en.short: Measuring excavation, disposal, fill, foundations, hardcore and damp-proofing under the local method.

sections.heading: Standard and scope
sections.text:
Substructure is the part below ground: foundations, excavation, fill and damp-proofing. The standard method of measurement is national.

In the UK, NRM2 is used for building works and CESMM4 for civil works. In Nigeria, confirm with the NIQS and the contract; do not assume a UK method. The method sets how items are described, grouped and measured, including depth bands, working space and waste.

sections.heading: Excavation and disposal
sections.text:
Excavation is measured in cubic metres as in situ volume before digging. Describe material, such as topsoil, ordinary soil or rock, and starting level. Depth is treated in bands or as extra over, as the method requires.

Working space is extra excavation beside foundations for formwork or construction. Measure it only when the method allows, and state the width. Surplus or unsuitable material is measured as disposal. Excavated soil may be reused as fill; the rest is wasted. Bulking is the increase in volume when soil is loosened, so loose volume is greater than in situ volume.

sections.heading: Filling, concrete and damp-proofing
sections.text:
Filling is measured as compacted volume. Say whether it is from excavated material or imported. Hardcore is broken stone or brick filling, measured in cubic metres.

Concrete foundations, such as strip and pad footings, are measured net in cubic metres from specified dimensions. Formwork to foundation sides is separate if required. Damp-proof course (DPC) and damp-proof membrane (DPM) are measured in square or linear metres, with laps and positions described.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A trench is 12 m long, 0.60 m wide and 1.00 m deep.
Volume = 12 × 0.60 × 1.00 = 7.20 m³.
If the method requires working space to be measured, a 0.30 m working space each side adds 0.60 m:
new width = 1.20 m, volume = 12 × 1.20 × 1.00 = 14.40 m³.
Working space = 14.40 − 7.20 = 7.20 m³.
If 5.00 m³ of the 14.40 m³ is reused, disposal = 14.40 − 5.00 = 9.40 m³ in situ.
Check whether the method measures disposal in situ or loose volume.

keyPoints: Measure excavation in cubic metres as in situ volume, describing material and depth.
Working space is extra excavation beside foundations and is measured only as the standard method allows.
Filling is measured as compacted volume; hardcore is filling measured in cubic metres.
Concrete foundations are measured net in cubic metres; DPC and DPM in square or linear metres.
Bulking increases loose volume, so check whether disposal is measured in situ or loose volume.
Use the national standard method, such as NRM2 in the UK, and confirm the Nigerian requirement with the NIQS and the contract.

en.title: Measurement of Superstructure
en.short: Measuring concrete frames, walls, floors, roofs, structural steel and timber, with deductions and descriptions.

sections.heading: Rules and take-off
sections.text:
Superstructure is the part of a building above the substructure: columns, beams, walls, floors and roof. Measurement, often called take-off, starts from drawings, schedules and the project’s method of measurement. Rules differ by country and client. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering, while quantity surveying registration is separate. Use the stated method and local code, not another country’s practice.

Work item by item. Describe material, grade or mix, size, thickness, level and workmanship. Group similar work so a contractor can price it.

sections.heading: Concrete frames and walls
sections.text:
Measure concrete separately from formwork and reinforcement. Concrete volume = length × width × thickness. Formwork is the contact area of the temporary mould. Reinforcement is measured by length or mass from bar schedules. Walls are measured by volume or area as the method requires, with openings deducted.

Complex shapes are split into rectangles, triangles or segments on a grid. Record gross quantities, then deduct openings and voids. A deduction must match the opening’s true size and depth.

sections.heading: Floors, roofs and timber
sections.text:
Floors and roofs may be slabs, beams, trusses or sheets. For sloping roofs, measure the true sloping area, not the plan area, unless the method says otherwise. Timber is described by species or grade, sawn size, length and treatment, and measured by length, area or volume. Trusses and complex roofs are taken member by member.

Structural steel is described by section, grade, length and connections, and measured by mass. Mass = length × mass per metre. Check the schedule against drawings.

sections.heading: Worked check
sections.text:
Example: a concrete slab is 6.0 m by 4.0 m by 0.15 m, with a 1.2 m by 0.9 m opening through it.
Gross concrete = 6.0 × 4.0 × 0.15 = 3.60 m³
Opening volume = 1.2 × 0.9 × 0.15 = 0.162 m³
Net concrete = 3.60 − 0.162 = 3.438 m³
Soffit formwork = (6.0 × 4.0) − (1.2 × 0.9) = 24 − 1.08 = 22.92 m²
Check units; round at the end.

keyPoints: Superstructure measurement covers frames, walls, floors, roofs, steel and timber above substructure.
Concrete, formwork and reinforcement are measured separately and described fully.
Net quantity = gross quantity − deductions for openings and voids.
Concrete volume = length × width × thickness; formwork is contact area.
Steel mass = length × mass per metre; timber is described by grade, size and treatment.
Use the project’s stated method of measurement and local rules, which differ by country.

en.title: Measurement of Finishes, Joinery and Fittings
en.short: Measuring finishes, joinery, fittings, glazing and painting, with openings and provisional items.

sections.heading: Measured work and finishes
sections.text:
Measured work is described and quantified under the project’s measurement rules, then priced in a bill of quantities. Finishes include plaster, screeds, tiling and floor coverings. They are usually measured in square metres; linear items such as skirting are measured in metres, and complete items in number. Many standards deduct openings above a stated size and make separate allowance for reveals and returns. The threshold and method differ by country and standard, so follow the rules named in the contract.

Example: a wall is 5.00 m long and 2.80 m high. Gross area = 5.00 × 2.80 = 14.00 m². Assume the project rule deducts a door opening 0.90 m × 2.10 m = 1.89 m². Net plaster area = 14.00 − 1.89 = 12.11 m². Measure each face separately if both are plastered.

sections.heading: Joinery, glazing and mouldings
sections.text: Joinery covers doors, windows, frames, linings, stair parts and built-in cupboards. Complete items, including frames and linings, are often enumerated, while trims such as skirting and architraves are measured by length. Describe timber or board type, finish and cross-section. Glazing is generally measured by area, stating glass type and thickness; small panes may be enumerated if the rules allow. Simple mouldings such as beads, architraves and cornices are measured in linear metres, with the profile described. Curved or special mouldings may be measured separately.

sections.heading: Fittings and provisional items
sections.text: Fittings are fixed manufactured items such as ironmongery, sanitary fittings and kitchen units. They may be enumerated and described, or covered by a provisional sum when the design is not final. A provisional sum is an allowance for work that cannot be measured yet; it is adjusted later when the work is finally measured and valued. A prime cost sum is an allowance for materials or equipment supplied by a named supplier. Painting and decoration are usually measured by area, stating the number of coats and surface preparation. The distinction matters: measured work is quantified, fittings are described or allowed for, and provisional items are estimates subject to later adjustment.

keyPoints: Measured work is quantified under the project’s measurement rules and priced in the bill of quantities.
Finishes are usually measured in square metres, linear trim in metres and complete items in number.
Net finish area = gross area − deducted openings, following the project’s rules for opening size and returns.
Joinery items are described and enumerated or measured by length; glazing is generally measured by area.
Fittings may be enumerated or covered by a provisional sum; provisional sums are adjusted later.
Painting and decoration are measured by area with coats and preparation stated.

en.title: Measurement of Building Services
en.short: Taking off plumbing, drainage, electrical and simple mechanical services from drawings and specifications.

sections.heading: Taking off services
sections.text: Building services are the pipes, drains, cables, conduits and equipment that make a building usable. Measurement, or taking off, means extracting quantities from drawings and specifications so they can be described and priced. A quantity surveyor does not measure services by cost. The quantity is the length, area, number or mass stated in the local method of measurement. Services rules and trade conventions differ by country, so always check the current local method before taking off.

sections.heading: Pipework and drainage
sections.text: Plumbing pipework is usually measured by length along the centreline and classified by material, diameter and jointing method. Fittings such as elbows, tees, reducers and valves are counted by number. Sanitary fixtures, tanks, pumps, manholes and gullies are enumerated, which means counted item by item. Drainage pipes are measured by length, with gradients and depths noted where the local rules require them. Underground drainage may be kept separate from above-ground work.

sections.heading: Electrical and mechanical
sections.text: Electrical conduit and cable are measured by length and classified by type and size. Switches, sockets, light points and other accessories are counted. Distribution boards, control panels and simple mechanical equipment such as fans or small pumps are enumerated. Ductwork may be measured by length or by surface area, depending on the local method. Builders’ work in connection, such as holes, chases and supports, may need separate measurement.

sections.heading: Rules and example
sections.text: Use the current local method and record every description clearly. A simple check: a cold-water branch runs 8 m + 5 m + 3 m = 16 m of pipe. It has two elbows, one tee and one valve. The pipe quantity is 16 m; the fittings are counted as two elbows, one tee and one valve. Do not add waste or overlap unless the local rules say so.

keyPoints: Taking off means extracting measured quantities from drawings and specifications.
Pipework is measured by length; fittings, fixtures and equipment are counted.
Cables and conduits are measured by length; accessories and boards are counted.
Ductwork may be measured by length or area, so follow the local method.
Services measurement rules and trade conventions differ by country; check the current local method.
Builders’ work in connection may need separate measurement.

en.title: Measurement of Civil Engineering Works
en.short: Measuring earthworks, roads, drainage and concrete by civil engineering conventions.

sections.heading: Civil versus building
sections.text: Civil engineering measurement uses the same units as building measurement, but the scale and method differ. Building bills often measure room by room from plans. Civil bills often work from longitudinal sections and cross-sections at chainages, which are distances along a road or pipeline. Quantities may be approximate and remeasured because ground conditions vary. The specified method matters: civil work in the UK may follow CESMM, the Civil Engineering Standard Method of Measurement. Codes and registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN (the engineering regulator) sets engineering practice. Check the contract’s method and local rules.

sections.heading: Earthworks and haulage
sections.text: Earthworks are measured in cubic metres of in situ material, classified by material and depth. Topsoil, ordinary soil and rock are kept separate. Excavation, filling, compaction, disposal and haulage are separate items. Volume between chainages can use the average end area rule: V = (A1 + A2) ÷ 2 × L. Example: areas 12 m² and 18 m², 100 m apart: V = (12 + 18) ÷ 2 × 100 = 1,500 m³. If bulking is 25%, loose volume for haulage = 1,500 × 1.25 = 1,875 m³. Bulking factor = loose volume ÷ in situ volume. Compaction reduces voids; check the specified compaction factor.

sections.heading: Roads and drainage
sections.text: Road layers are measured by area (m²), or by volume where thickness varies. Lengths are referenced to chainage. Drainage pipes are measured by length, classified by diameter, material, bedding, surround and depth to invert, the pipe’s lowest internal level. Manholes and gullies are counted or measured by depth. Excavation, backfill and disposal may be measured as separate items or included in the pipework items, depending on the measurement method.

sections.heading: Concrete structures
sections.text: Simple concrete structures such as culverts, retaining walls and small bridges are measured as concrete volume (m³), formwork area of contact surface (m²) and reinforcement mass (kg or tonne). A bar bending schedule lists bars by size, shape and length. Joints, bearings and waterproofing are separate items. Civil measurement stresses method-related items, temporary works and haulage more than building measurement.

keyPoints: Civil measurement often uses chainages and cross-sections, not room-by-room building take-off.
Earthwork volume between sections: V = (A1 + A2) ÷ 2 × L.
Bulking factor = loose volume ÷ in situ volume; haulage volume = in situ volume × bulking factor.
Road layers are measured by area or volume; drainage pipes by length with depth and bedding classes.
Concrete is measured by volume, formwork by contact area and reinforcement by mass.
Check the specified method and national rules; codes, standards and registration differ by country.

en.title: Preparing and pricing bills of quantities
en.short: Taking off, abstracting, billing, and the parts of a bill of quantities.

sections.heading: Take-off to billing
sections.text: A bill of quantities (BoQ) is a document that lists the work in a project, usually with quantities and descriptions, so tenderers can price it on the same basis. The quantity surveyor moves through three stages. Taking off measures dimensions from drawings and schedules. Abstracting collects like items, adds the quantities and checks units. Billing writes the descriptions and quantities in bill order. Tenderers then price the items and the totals are cast up. Each stage must be checked against the previous one.

sections.heading: Parts of a bill
sections.text: Preambles are introductory statements: project description, specification references, measurement rules and site conditions. Preliminaries are priced items for site management, temporary works, insurance and supervision. Measured work covers the permanent works, measured under the project’s method of measurement. Provisional sums are allowances for work not yet fully defined. Dayworks pay for work by recorded labour, plant and materials at agreed rates, often when work cannot be measured in advance. The order can vary, but these parts are common.

sections.heading: Billing arithmetic
sections.text: A take-off gives 12.5 m³ of concrete. The abstract carries 12.5 m³. In the bill it is priced at 80,000 per m³: 12.5 × 80,000 = 1,000,000. Add preliminaries 150,000, a provisional sum 300,000 and dayworks 50,000. Bill total = 1,000,000 + 150,000 + 300,000 + 50,000 = 1,500,000. The rates are illustrative; current rates vary by place and time.

sections.heading: Formats vary
sections.text: Standard methods and bill formats differ by country and client. The UK has the RICS New Rules of Measurement (NRM) for building work and CESMM for civil engineering; many Commonwealth countries use adapted or client-specific formats. Always read the project’s method of measurement and preamble before billing. Do not assume one country’s format applies elsewhere.

keyPoints: A bill of quantities lists work so tenderers price the same items.
The chain is taking off, then abstracting, then billing.
Preambles state rules and conditions; preliminaries are priced site and management items.
Provisional sums cover undefined work; dayworks pay by recorded labour, plant and materials.
Bill total = measured work + preliminaries + provisional sums + dayworks, with other additions as the bill requires.
Standard methods and bill formats vary by country and client, so check the project’s method of measurement.

en.title: Estimating and Cost Planning
en.short: Building unit rates from resources, and using approximate estimates and cost plans at design stages.

sections.heading: Building unit rates
sections.text:
A unit rate is the price of one unit of work, such as one cubic metre of concrete. It is built up from material, labour, plant, overheads and profit. Material cost is quantity times price, with an allowance for waste. Labour cost uses a labour constant, the time needed per unit, multiplied by the wage rate. Plant cost is hire or ownership cost per hour multiplied by hours per unit. Overheads and profit are added as a percentage of direct cost.

Illustrative example for 1 m³ of concrete: material 80.00, labour constant 2.5 hours at 8.00 per hour = 20.00, plant 30.00 per hour at 5 m³ per hour = 6.00. Direct cost = 80 + 20 + 6 = 106.00. Add 15% overheads and profit = 15.90. Unit rate = 121.90.

sections.heading: Approximate estimating
sections.text: At brief and concept stages there may be no drawings to measure. Approximate estimating uses past cost data. Common methods are the unit method (cost per bed or per pupil), the square metre method (cost per m² of floor area), the cube method (cost per m³ of building volume) and elemental estimating (cost per element such as frame or finishes). Adjust the data for location, time, size and quality. The result is a range, not a precise price.

sections.heading: Cost planning and checks
sections.text:
A cost limit is the client’s budget ceiling. A cost plan divides that limit among building elements. A cost check compares the designed cost with the plan or limit and prompts redesign if needed. Cost planning is iterative: estimate, check, adjust.

Use current local rates. Material prices, wages and labour constants change with time and place, so old or foreign data can mislead. Check rates against recent local projects and supplier quotations, and state the date and location of any cost data.

keyPoints: A unit rate is built up from material, labour, plant, overheads and profit.
Labour cost per unit = labour constant × wage rate; plant cost per unit = plant hourly rate ÷ output per hour.
Approximate estimating uses unit, square metre, cube or elemental methods when drawings are incomplete.
A cost limit is the client’s budget ceiling; a cost plan allocates it to elements; a cost check compares design cost with the plan.
Use current local rates because prices, wages and labour constants change with time and place.
State the date and location of cost data and adjust for location, time, size and quality.

en.title: Tendering and Procurement
en.short: Procurement methods, tender documents, tendering, bid evaluation and common contract types.

sections.heading: Procurement methods
sections.text: Procurement is how a client obtains design and construction. Methods include open tendering, where any qualified firm may bid; selective tendering, where a shortlist is invited; negotiated procurement, where the client bargains with firms; and direct award in special cases. Design and build gives one contractor responsibility for design and construction. Public procurement rules and thresholds differ by country. In Nigeria, federal public procurement is governed by the Public Procurement Act 2007; state and other countries’ rules differ, so use the current official rules.

sections.heading: Tender documents
sections.text: Tender documents tell bidders what to price and how bids will be judged. They usually include the invitation to tender, instructions to tenderers, form of tender, conditions of contract, drawings, specification, bills of quantities or schedule of rates, forms of agreement and bond, and evaluation criteria. A bill of quantities lets bidders price measured work; a schedule of rates suits work whose quantities are uncertain. Documents must be clear and consistent, because ambiguity leads to claims.

sections.heading: Tendering and evaluation
sections.text: Tendering usually follows prequalification or a capacity check, then invitation, site visit, queries, submission, public opening, evaluation and award. Evaluation first checks compliance, then technical capacity and price; arithmetic errors are corrected and confirmed with the bidder before prices are compared. The lowest evaluated bid is not always the lowest price: value for money, programme, quality and risk count. Example: bids of 120,000,000 and 115,000,000 naira are checked. The second has a 3,000,000 naira arithmetic error understated, so its corrected price is 118,000,000. It remains lower, but only if it passes technical checks.

sections.heading: Contract types
sections.text: Contract types include lump sum, where a fixed price covers defined work; measured or re-measurement, where payment follows actual quantities at agreed rates; cost plus, where the client pays actual cost plus a fee; and target cost, where savings or overruns are shared. Design and build and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts place design and construction risk with the contractor. Framework agreements allow repeat work. Choice depends on design certainty, risk allocation and the client’s capacity to manage.

keyPoints: Procurement method is how a client buys design and construction; contract type is how risk and payment are allocated.
Tender documents must be complete and consistent; they include instructions, conditions, drawings, specification, bills of quantities or schedule of rates and evaluation criteria.
Open tendering invites any qualified bidder; selective tendering invites a shortlist; negotiated and direct award need justification.
Bid evaluation checks compliance and technical capacity before comparing prices, with arithmetic errors corrected and confirmed; the lowest evaluated bid may not be the lowest price.
Common contract types are lump sum, measured or re-measurement, cost plus, target cost, design and build and EPC.
Public procurement rules and thresholds differ by country; use the current official rules, such as Nigeria’s Public Procurement Act 2007 for federal procurement.

en.title: Construction Contracts and Law
en.short: How construction contracts are formed, performed, breached and remedied under Nigerian law and standard forms.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.text:
A contract is a legally binding agreement. In Nigeria, construction contracts are governed mainly by common law and statute, not by one contract code. Formation needs offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity and certainty. In tendering, the invitation to tender is usually an invitation to treat, that is an invitation to negotiate rather than an offer; the contractor’s tender is the offer; the client’s letter of acceptance is the acceptance. A signed contract or a letter of acceptance can create the binding agreement, but check which documents form the contract.

Case: Adaeze Ltd invites tenders for a school block in Enugu. Bello Construction tenders ₦48,000,000. Adaeze accepts in writing. There is offer, acceptance and consideration: Bello will build, Adaeze will pay. If Adaeze later refuses site access, that may breach an express or implied term to give possession.

sections.heading: Obligations and standard forms
sections.text: The contractor must carry out the works with reasonable skill, to the specification and within the time. The employer must pay, give possession of the site and co-operate. Standard forms allocate risk in advance. FIDIC is widely used internationally; JCT is the main United Kingdom family; NEC4 is the current edition of the NEC family, which began in the United Kingdom and is also used abroad. Nigerian public projects often use government conditions, while private projects may adapt FIDIC or JCT. Names and editions matter, so read the actual form. A bill of quantities, drawings, specification and conditions are usually contract documents.

sections.heading: Breach and remedies
sections.text: Breach includes late completion, defective work, late payment or wrongful termination. Remedies include damages for proven loss, termination, and specific performance, which is rare. Liquidated damages must be a genuine pre-estimate of loss, not a penalty. Example: suppose the contract sets ₦20,000 per day for delay. Thirty days late gives 30 × ₦20,000 = ₦600,000, if the clause is enforceable. The innocent party must mitigate the loss, that is take reasonable steps to reduce it.

sections.heading: Legal framework
sections.text: In Nigeria, the Public Procurement Act 2007 regulates federal public procurement; state laws differ. The Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 governs arbitration. Other countries have their own statutes and standard forms. Always check the law and form of the project’s country.

keyPoints: A construction contract needs offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, capacity and certainty.
In tendering, the tender is usually the offer and the letter of acceptance is the acceptance.
Standard forms such as FIDIC, JCT and NEC4 allocate risk; Nigerian public and private projects may use different forms.
Breach gives the innocent party damages for proven loss, and sometimes termination.
Liquidated damages must be a genuine pre-estimate, not a penalty.
Nigerian federal public procurement is regulated by the Public Procurement Act 2007; state and other country rules differ.

en.title: Contract Administration and Valuation
en.short: Interim valuations, payment certificates, variations, instructions, records and final accounts.

sections.heading: Interim valuations
sections.text: An interim valuation is a periodic assessment of work done and materials on site. The quantity surveyor measures executed work, applies contract rates, adds agreed variations, deducts previous payments and retention, and prepares the valuation for certification. Retention is a percentage held back to secure performance. Payment rules, certificate procedures and who may certify differ by country and contract, so check the contract and current official guidance.

sections.heading: Certificates and instructions
sections.text: A payment certificate is the certifier’s formal statement that a sum is due. The certifier may be the engineer, architect or contract administrator, depending on the contract. An instruction is a formal direction to the contractor. It should be in writing; if given orally, confirm it in writing at once. Only instructed changes should be valued as variations. A variation is a change to scope, quality or timing, valued at contract rates or, where rates do not apply, by fair valuation.

sections.heading: Records and final account
sections.text: Good records support every valuation: site diaries, measurement sheets, instructions, correspondence, delivery notes and daywork sheets. They show what was done, when and under whose instruction. The final account is the agreed statement of the final contract sum. It brings together the original contract sum, all variations, adjustments and agreed claims. The QS checks and agrees it with the contractor before the final certificate.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
An interim valuation shows work done ₦8,000,000 and materials on site ₦500,000, which the contract allows. Previous payments are ₦3,000,000. Retention is 5% of work done, not materials.
Gross value = 8,000,000 + 500,000 = 8,500,000
Retention = 5% × 8,000,000 = 400,000
Net due = 8,500,000 − 400,000 − 3,000,000 = 5,100,000
The certificate should state the sum due and the basis. The contract may treat retention differently, so check it.

keyPoints: An interim valuation measures work done and materials on site to support periodic payment.
Net payment = gross value − retention − previous payments, subject to the contract.
A payment certificate is the certifier’s formal statement of the sum due; who certifies and the time limits vary by country and contract.
Instructions should be written; oral instructions should be confirmed in writing immediately.
Variations are valued at contract rates where applicable, otherwise by fair valuation.
The final account reconciles the contract sum with all variations, adjustments and agreed claims.

en.title: Claims, Delay and Dispute Resolution
en.short: Causes of claims, delay and disruption, extension of time, loss and expense, and dispute resolution methods.

sections.heading: Claims and causes
sections.text: A construction claim is a request for more time or more money under the contract. Common causes include variations, late issue of drawings or information, delayed possession of the site, unforeseen ground conditions, exceptionally bad weather, late payment and design changes. The contract and its standard form allocate these risks. Forms such as FIDIC, JCT or NEC allocate risk, but edition and amendments matter. A claim must normally be notified within a stated period, so record events and keep contemporary records.

sections.heading: Delay, disruption, time and money
sections.text:
Delay means work finishes later than planned. Disruption means lower productivity, for example crowded access or repeated changes, and it can happen without overall delay. An extension of time (EOT) moves the completion date for an excusable delay. It usually protects the contractor from liquidated damages, pre-agreed damages for late completion. Loss and expense recovers prolongation (the cost of staying on site longer) and disruption costs, such as site staff and plant, if the employer caused it and the contract allows.

Example: completion is due on 30 June. The employer delays possession by 42 days. An EOT of 42 days moves completion to 11 August. Site overheads are ₦120,000 per week. Six weeks of prolongation give 6 × ₦120,000 = ₦720,000, claimed as loss and expense if proved.

sections.heading: Dispute resolution methods
sections.text:
Negotiation is direct discussion and keeps control with the parties. Mediation uses an independent mediator to help them settle; it is not binding unless they sign an agreement. Adjudication gives a quick interim decision from an adjudicator, often binding until final resolution. Arbitration is a private tribunal whose award is usually binding and enforceable. Litigation is court proceedings, which are public and binding but can be slow.

Procedures vary by country. The UK has statutory adjudication for construction contracts under the Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996. Nigeria’s Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 governs arbitration and mediation. In many countries adjudication is contractual, not statutory. Always check the governing law, the contract and the seat of the arbitration (its legal home).

keyPoints: A claim is a request for extra time or money under the contract; common causes are variations, late information, delayed possession and unforeseen conditions.
Delay extends completion, while disruption lowers productivity and may not extend the whole project.
An extension of time moves the completion date; revised completion = original completion + excusable delay.
Loss and expense recovers proved prolongation costs; for a simple case, loss and expense = weekly cost × weeks.
Negotiation and mediation are consensual; adjudication is a quick interim decision; arbitration and litigation are binding.
Adjudication, arbitration and court rules differ by country, so check the governing law and the contract.

en.title: Cost Control and Cash Flow
en.short: Cost reporting, committed and actual cost, forecast final cost, cash flow, S-curves and simple earned value.

sections.heading: Cost reporting and control
sections.text: Cost control compares what has been spent and committed with the budget, then forecasts the final cost. Actual cost is the cost of work done and certified or invoiced. Committed cost is the value of orders and subcontracts placed but not yet certified or invoiced; it is a liability before cash leaves. Forecast final cost = actual cost to date + committed cost not yet certified + estimated cost to complete + known adjustments. Cost reports show these figures against budget, with variances and a cost value reconciliation. Control means acting on the variances: change scope, renegotiate, accelerate or slow work.

sections.heading: Cash flow and S-curves
sections.text: Cash flow forecasting shows money in and out over time. The client pays the contractor, often monthly against certificates, and may hold retention; the contractor pays labour, suppliers and subcontractors. A contractor can be profitable and still fail if payments arrive after its bills. The client needs cash flow to plan funding and avoid late payment. An S-curve plots cumulative cost or progress against time: slow at the start, steep in the middle, slow at the end. Comparing planned and actual S-curves shows delay or overspend. Payment and retention rules differ by contract and country, so check the conditions.

sections.heading: Simple earned value
sections.text: Simple earned value compares planned value (PV), earned value (EV) and actual cost (AC). PV is the budget for work planned by now; EV is the budget for work actually done; AC is what it cost. Cost variance CV = EV − AC. Schedule variance SV = EV − PV. Cost performance index CPI = EV ÷ AC; schedule performance index SPI = EV ÷ PV. Example: budget 1,200,000; at month 3 PV = 300,000, EV = 250,000, AC = 280,000. CV = −30,000 (over budget); SV = −50,000 (behind). CPI = 250,000 ÷ 280,000 = 0.893; SPI = 250,000 ÷ 300,000 = 0.833. Forecast final cost = budget ÷ CPI = 1,200,000 ÷ 0.893 = 1,344,000 approximately.

keyPoints: Actual cost is work certified or invoiced; committed cost is ordered work not yet certified or invoiced.
Forecast final cost = actual cost to date + committed cost not yet certified + estimated cost to complete + known adjustments.
Cash flow forecasting matters because payments lag costs, so a profitable contractor can still run short of cash.
An S-curve plots cumulative cost or progress against time and is compared with the plan.
CV = EV − AC and SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV ÷ AC and SPI = EV ÷ PV.
Forecast final cost using CPI = budget ÷ CPI, but this simple method assumes the same efficiency continues.

en.title: Project Management and Risk for Quantity Surveyors
en.short: Planning, scheduling, risk registers, expected value, quality and safety for cost and time advice.

sections.heading: Planning and scheduling
sections.text:
Planning decides what must be done, in what order and by when. A work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the project into packages. Scheduling turns the plan into a programme with dates. The critical path method (CPM) finds the longest chain of dependent activities. That chain is the critical path and has zero float. Float is the time an activity can slip without delaying the project. A Gantt chart shows activities as bars.

The quantity surveyor (QS) links the programme to money. Time-related preliminaries, such as site staff and plant, cost more when the programme lengthens. The QS uses the programme to forecast cash flow and value work at interim stages.

sections.heading: Risk analysis
sections.text:
Risk is an uncertain event that may affect cost, time or quality. The QS helps to build a risk register: a list of risks with cause, probability, impact and owner. Simple analysis multiplies probability by impact to give expected monetary value (EMV). Mitigation reduces probability or impact; a risk allowance or contingency is money set aside for remaining risk.

Example: risk A has probability 20% and impact ₦5,000,000. Risk B has probability 10% and impact ₦12,000,000.
EMV A = 0.20 × ₦5,000,000 = ₦1,000,000
EMV B = 0.10 × ₦12,000,000 = ₦1,200,000
Total risk allowance = ₦2,200,000. It is a planning figure.

sections.heading: Quality and safety
sections.text:
Quality assurance is the system that prevents defects. Quality control checks the work by inspection and testing. The QS prices these checks and the cost of rework and snagging. Snagging is finding and listing defects near handover.

Health and safety law differs by country. In the UK, the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations place duties on clients, designers and contractors. In Nigeria, the Factories Act and related regulations address workplace safety. The QS checks safety costs in the estimate.

sections.heading: QS advice
sections.text:
The QS reports cost, time and risk together. Change control tests each change against the programme and the risk allowance.

Good advice separates known cost from uncertain risk.

keyPoints: A WBS breaks work into packages; a programme adds dates and dependencies.
The critical path is the longest dependent chain and has zero float; float is spare time before a delay affects completion.
A risk register records cause, probability, impact and owner; EMV = probability × impact.
Risk allowance = sum of EMVs; it is a planning figure, not a guarantee.
Quality assurance prevents defects; quality control inspects and tests; snagging lists defects at handover.
Health and safety duties differ by country; the QS must include safety costs in estimates and cost reports.

en.title: Property Development and Feasibility
en.short: Development process, site appraisal, feasibility, cost advice, valuation and investment appraisal.

sections.heading: Development process
sections.text: Property development is the process of buying or optioning land, obtaining planning or development approval, designing, financing, building and selling or letting the completed property. It runs through appraisal, feasibility, design, procurement, construction and disposal. Planning rules, building codes and approval bodies differ by country. In Nigeria, for example, development approval involves state or local planning authorities; check current official requirements.

sections.heading: Site appraisal
sections.text: Site appraisal tests whether a site can carry the intended scheme. It covers location and demand, access, services, ground conditions, contamination, flooding, title and planning constraints. Surveys and professional reports reduce risk. Local market evidence and official planning guidance must be used because values and rules vary by country and time.

sections.heading: Feasibility and cost
sections.text: A feasibility study asks whether the scheme is worthwhile. It compares gross development value (GDV, the expected sale or rental value) with total development cost (TDC): construction, professional fees, finance, contingency and taxes. Cost advice from a quantity surveyor gives early estimates and a cost plan. Residual land value = GDV − TDC − required developer’s profit; the residual is the most the scheme can pay for the land. If the residual is below the asking price, the scheme is weak. Figures change, so use current local data.

sections.heading: Valuation and appraisal
sections.text: Simple valuation uses the income method: capital value = net operating income (annual rent less operating expenses) ÷ capitalisation rate (the required income yield). Example: net operating income ₦1,200,000 a year and a rate of 8% give 1,200,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₦15,000,000. Investment appraisal discounts future cash flows. Net present value (NPV) = Σ cash flow ÷ (1 + r)^t − initial cost. Example: cost ₦10,000,000, inflows ₦4,000,000 for three years, r = 10%. NPV = 4,000,000 ÷ 1.1 + 4,000,000 ÷ 1.1² + 4,000,000 ÷ 1.1³ − 10,000,000 = −₦52,600 approximately. A negative NPV fails the test at that rate. Payback and internal rate of return (the discount rate giving zero NPV) are also used. Methods and markets differ by country.

keyPoints: Feasibility compares gross development value with total development cost and required developer’s profit.
Residual land value is GDV − TDC − required developer’s profit, with land excluded from TDC.
Capital value is net operating income ÷ capitalisation rate.
NPV = Σ cash flow ÷ (1 + r)^t − initial cost; a positive NPV adds value at the chosen discount rate.
Site appraisal checks access, services, ground conditions, title and planning constraints before design.
Planning rules, valuation methods and property market data differ by country, so use current local official sources.

en.title: Professional Practice and Ethics in Quantity Surveying
en.short: Duties, ethics, liability, confidentiality, conflicts of interest and the bodies that regulate quantity surveyors.

sections.heading: Duties and standards
sections.text:
Professional practice covers how a quantity surveyor (QS) works and the standards they are expected to meet. A QS owes the client a duty of care: to work with the skill and care of a reasonably competent practitioner in the same field. That covers measurement, cost advice, tender documents and valuations. Duties also run to the public and to contractors who rely on those documents.

Keeping records, checking figures and updating skills through continuing professional development (CPD) are part of the duty.

sections.heading: Ethics and conflicts
sections.text:
Ethics are the principles that guide conduct: honesty, integrity, competence, objectivity and confidentiality. Confidentiality means client information is not passed on without permission, except where the law requires disclosure. A conflict of interest arises when a personal or financial interest could sway professional judgement. The usual rule is to disclose it in writing and manage it openly.

Case: Adaeze, a QS in Lagos, is offered a share of a supply contract if she specifies one supplier’s blocks. She declines and records the approach.

sections.heading: Liability
sections.text:
Liability is legal responsibility for loss caused by a failure. A QS may be liable in contract, for breaking agreed terms, or in negligence, for falling below the standard of care. Wrong quantities, missed items or careless cost advice can lead to claims. Professional indemnity (PI) insurance covers such claims up to a stated limit.

Limitation periods, which set how long a claim may be brought, and caps on liability differ by country, so check local law and the policy.

sections.heading: Bodies and regulators
sections.text:
Professional bodies set entry standards, codes of conduct, CPD requirements and disciplinary processes. Examples are RICS in the UK, AIQS in Australia and NIQS in Nigeria. Some countries also have a statutory regulator. In Nigeria, the Quantity Surveyors Registration Board of Nigeria (QSRBN) registers practitioners by law, while NIQS is the professional institute. COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria, not quantity surveying.

Protected titles and the rules on who may practise differ by country, so check current national requirements.

keyPoints: A QS owes a duty of care at the level of a reasonably competent practitioner.
Confidentiality, honesty and objectivity are core ethical duties; disclose conflicts of interest in writing.
Liability may arise in contract or in negligence, and professional indemnity insurance covers claims up to a limit.
RICS (UK), AIQS (Australia) and NIQS (Nigeria) are professional bodies; QSRBN is Nigeria’s statutory registration board.
COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria, not quantity surveying.
Registration rules, protected titles and limitation periods differ by country; check the current national requirements.

en.title: Final-Year Project in Quantity Surveying
en.short: Planning, literature, data, ethics, honesty and presenting a supervised quantity surveying project.

sections.heading: Defining and planning
sections.text: A final-year project is a supervised piece of independent work on a quantity surveying problem. Start by turning a broad interest into a focused question that can be answered with the time and data available. Suppose Ada, a final-year student at a Nigerian polytechnic, studies how variation orders affect final accounts on small public building projects. She writes a proposal with question, aims, objectives, method, data sources, timeline and risks. Plan backwards from the submission date, set milestones and meet your supervisor regularly. Keep a project log of meetings, decisions and sources.

sections.heading: Evidence and honesty
sections.text: Review literature that is relevant to the question, not everything written about construction. Use textbooks, journal articles, official reports and reliable professional sources, and record full references as you read. Match the method to the question: interviews, questionnaires, document analysis, case studies or a mix. Pilot instruments where possible. Collect data systematically and analyse it in a way that answers the question. Keep raw data, consent forms and analysis files in an orderly folder, with backups. Academic honesty means no plagiarism, no fabricated data and no unacknowledged help. Cite others and report results that do not support your expectation. Ethics approval rules are set by your institution and country. If your work involves people or personal data, obtain approval before collecting data, seek informed consent, protect anonymity and store data securely. In Nigeria, check your university or polytechnic ethics committee or departmental procedure.

sections.heading: Report and presentation
sections.text: Write the report in a clear structure: introduction, literature review, method, results, discussion, conclusion, references and appendices. Use tables and figures only when they help. In the oral presentation, explain the question, method, main findings and limitations in the time allowed. Do not read slides. Expect questions on sampling, bias and ethics, and answer honestly. A good project shows careful reasoning and a clear trail from question to evidence to conclusion.

keyPoints: A final-year project answers a focused, feasible quantity surveying question under supervision.
Plan milestones backwards from the submission date and keep a log of meetings, decisions and sources.
The literature review should be relevant and referenced as you read.
Match the method to the question, collect data systematically and analyse it to answer the question.

Academic honesty forbids plagiarism, fabricated data and unacknowledged help; ethics approval is needed before collecting data involving people or personal information, and rules vary by institution and country.
Present the question, method, findings and limitations clearly and answer questions honestly.

en.title: Advanced Construction Economics: Models, Whole Life and Risk
en.short: Cost models, whole-life costing, risk, productivity, inflation and construction market behaviour.

sections.heading: Cost modelling
sections.text:
Cost modelling links design and quantities to price. A cost model relates building characteristics to cost. It may be parametric (cost per square metre), resource-based (labour, plant, materials) or probabilistic. Models are country-specific and time-sensitive: the same building costs different amounts in different places and dates. Use current indices from the national statistics office or a recognised cost consultant, and state base date and location.

Index adjustment: adjusted cost = base cost × (new index ÷ base index). Example: 48,000,000 naira at index 120 becomes 48,000,000 × (150 ÷ 120) = 60,000,000 naira at index 150.

sections.heading: Whole-life costing
sections.text:
Whole-life costing (WLC) compares options over the asset’s life, not only capital cost.
