It discounts future costs to present value: WLC = initial cost + Σ [future cost ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ] − residual value ÷ (1 + r)ᴺ. r is the discount rate; n is the year. The rate is a policy choice and differs by country.

Example: option A costs 10,000,000 now and 1,000,000 in year 1. At r = 10%, WLC = 10,000,000 + 1,000,000 ÷ 1.10 = 10,909,091. Option B costs 11,500,000 now. A is cheaper by 590,909.

sections.heading: Risk and uncertainty
sections.text: Risk is measurable variability; uncertainty is not. Expected value = probability × impact. For a 20% chance of a 5,000,000 naira loss, expected cost = 0.20 × 5,000,000 = 1,000,000 naira. Add expected values to a risk allowance, but avoid double-counting contingency. Sensitivity analysis changes one variable at a time; Monte Carlo simulation samples many variables together. Both need reliable data and stated assumptions.

sections.heading: Productivity and markets
sections.text: Productivity = output ÷ input, such as square metres of wall per labour hour. Construction productivity is hard to measure because projects differ. Inflation raises input prices; use construction-specific indices, not only consumer price inflation. Market behaviour includes demand cycles, competition and tender price levels. In booms, tenders may rise faster than costs; in downturns, contractors may price low to win work. Use current local data and date.

keyPoints: Cost models and indices are country-specific and time-sensitive; use current published data and state the base date and location.
Index adjustment: adjusted cost = base cost × (new index ÷ base index).
Whole-life cost: initial cost + Σ [future cost ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ] − residual value ÷ (1 + r)ᴺ.
Expected value = probability × impact; add expected values to a risk allowance without double-counting contingency.
Productivity = output ÷ input; construction inflation should be measured with construction-specific indices.
Market behaviour affects tender prices: booms can push tenders above cost inflation, downturns can produce low bids.

en.title: Digital Quantity Surveying and Building Information Modelling
en.short: BIM, 5D cost models, automated take-off, data analytics and checking digital outputs.

sections.heading: BIM and 5D
sections.text: Building information modelling (BIM) is a shared digital model of a built asset, with objects carrying geometry and data. ISO 19650 is an international standard for managing information through the asset life cycle. A 5D cost model adds cost to three-dimensional geometry and time: 3D plus time is 4D, and 5D adds cost. The model can link quantities to rates, but the link is only as good as the model and the rate library.

sections.heading: Automated take-off
sections.text: Automated take-off extracts quantities from model objects, such as concrete volumes or wall areas. Example: 20 columns, each 300 mm × 300 mm × 3.0 m. Volume per column = 0.3 × 0.3 × 3.0 = 0.27 m³. Total = 20 × 0.27 = 5.4 m³. At an illustrative ₦120,000/m³, cost = 5.4 × 120,000 = ₦648,000. The QS must check whether the rule measures net concrete, excludes openings, or treats waste in the rate.

sections.heading: Data and information
sections.text: Data analytics compares cost, quantity and time data across projects to benchmark and forecast. Digital information management uses a common data environment (CDE) to control versions, approvals and access. Open formats such as IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) help different software exchange models. Good information management records who changed what, when and why.

sections.heading: Limits and checking
sections.text: Automation does not replace judgement. Models may omit temporary works, site conditions, specification requirements or items not modelled. Object classification and measurement rules may not match local practice. Software can duplicate or miss objects. Check outputs against the applicable measurement rules, the specification and local labour and material practice. Keep an audit trail. Measurement rules, standards and professional regulation differ by country; for example, the RICS New Rules of Measurement are used in the UK.

keyPoints: BIM is a shared digital model with geometry and data; 5D adds cost to 3D and time.
Automated take-off is only as reliable as the model and its object data.
Column concrete volume = length × width × height × number; cost = quantity × rate.
Check model quantities against measurement rules, specifications and local practice.
Data analytics supports benchmarking but needs clean, comparable cost data.
ISO 19650 and a common data environment help control information versions and approvals.

en.title: Sustainable Construction and Carbon Costing
en.short: Sustainability, life-cycle assessment, carbon accounting, green procurement and low-carbon cost choices.

sections.heading: Sustainability and LCA
sections.text: Sustainability in construction means meeting present needs without harming future generations’ ability to meet theirs. For a QS, it affects cost planning, specification and value. Life-cycle assessment (LCA) is a structured method to estimate environmental impacts over a product or building’s life. ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 set out the international framework. Stages usually include raw material, manufacture, transport, construction, use and end of life. A cradle-to-gate study stops at the factory gate; cradle-to-grave includes use and disposal. Compare like with like because assumptions change results.

sections.heading: Carbon accounting and costing
sections.text: Carbon accounting measures greenhouse gas emissions in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e). It separates embodied carbon (from materials and construction) from operational carbon (from energy in use). An environmental product declaration (EPD) reports a product’s impacts, often under EN 15804 in Europe. Carbon costing puts money beside emissions. A simple measure is cost per tonne of CO2e saved. Example: a made-up Lagos office project can spend an extra ₦12,000,000 to cut embodied carbon by 800 tCO2e. The cost is 12,000,000 ÷ 800 = ₦15,000 per tCO2e. If the ceiling is ₦10,000 per tCO2e, that option fails. This is a marginal abatement cost, the cost of the next tonne avoided. Low-carbon choices may raise capital cost but lower whole-life cost through energy savings; carbon prices differ by country.

sections.heading: Green procurement and standards
sections.text: Green procurement means buying goods and services with environmental criteria as well as price and quality. It can include recycled content, low-carbon concrete, certified timber and energy-efficient plant. Rating tools and carbon standards vary by country and change over time. Examples include BREEAM (originally UK), LEED (originally US), Green Star (originally Australia) and EDGE (from the International Finance Corporation). Check the current version and local scheme before quoting a score or limit. In Nigeria, the public procurement framework and building codes set local rules; verify current editions. A QS should record assumptions, use verified EPDs where available, and treat green claims as costed options, not slogans.

keyPoints: Sustainability balances present needs with future needs and affects cost planning.
LCA follows ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 and can be cradle-to-gate or cradle-to-grave.
Carbon accounting reports tCO2e and separates embodied from operational carbon.
Cost per tonne CO2e saved = extra cost ÷ carbon saved.
Green procurement adds environmental criteria to price and quality, and rating tools vary by country.
Low-carbon options can raise capital cost but lower whole-life cost; check current local standards and carbon prices.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation in Quantity Surveying
en.short: Research design, literature review, methods, sampling, analysis, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Research design
sections.text:
Research design is the plan linking your question to evidence. It states aim, objectives, scope and method. Exploratory design suits a little-studied problem; descriptive design measures what exists; explanatory design tests causes. Quantitative methods use numbers and measurement; qualitative methods use words and meanings; mixed methods combine both. Choose the design that fits the question.

Case: Ada studies cost overruns on public building projects in Enugu, Nigeria. She asks what causes overruns and how large they are, so she uses a mixed design.

sections.heading: Evidence and sampling
sections.text:
A literature review is a critical synthesis of existing work, not a list of summaries. Search journals, government reports and professional publications; group findings by theme; identify the gap your study fills.

Sampling is selecting cases or people. Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection and supports generalisation; non-probability sampling does not give known chances, and purposive sampling, one form of it, selects information-rich cases. Ada sends questionnaires to 120 randomly selected quantity surveyors and gets 90 usable replies. Response rate = 90 ÷ 120 = 75%. She also interviews eight experienced surveyors purposively.

sections.heading: Analysis and ethics
sections.text:
Qualitative data can be analysed by thematic analysis: code the text, group codes into themes, and check themes against the raw data. Quantitative data can be analysed with descriptive statistics (means, percentages) and, where justified, inferential tests.

Research ethics covers informed consent, voluntary participation, anonymity, confidentiality and honest reporting. Ethics approval and data protection rules vary by institution and country, so check your university’s ethics committee and the data protection law where you collect data. Ada obtains approval before fieldwork, anonymises firms and stores files securely.

sections.heading: Writing the dissertation
sections.text:
A dissertation is an argument, not a report of activity. A common structure is introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references.

Keep one thread: each objective should be answered by a method and a result. Discuss limitations honestly. Cite every source and follow your institution’s style. Write early, revise, and ask your supervisor to review drafts.

keyPoints: Research design links the research question to evidence through a stated aim, objectives and method.
A literature review synthesises sources by theme and identifies the gap the study fills.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; purposive sampling selects information-rich cases.
Response rate = usable replies ÷ questionnaires sent × 100%.
Thematic analysis codes qualitative text into themes; descriptive statistics summarise quantitative data.
Ethics approval and data protection rules vary by institution and country, so check before fieldwork.
